articles.title: National Weather Alert: बंगाल की खाड़ी में चक्रवाती तूफान का खतरा, 6 राज्यों में भारी बारिश का अलर्ट; तमिलनाडु-केरल में रेड अलर्ट - People's Update

National Weather Alert: बंगाल की खाड़ी में चक्रवाती तूफान का खतरा, 6 राज्यों में भारी बारिश का अलर्ट; तमिलनाडु-केरल में रेड अलर्ट
बंगाल की खाड़ी में बन रहे कम दबाव के क्षेत्र के कारण देश के कई राज्यों में मौसम बदलने की आशंका है। मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के मुताबिक, यह सिस्टम 26 अक्टूबर तक चक्रवाती तूफान में बदल सकता है और 28 अक्टूबर के आसपास उत्तरी आंध्र प्रदेश तथा उससे सटे दक्षिणी ओडिशा के तटों की ओर बढ़ सकता है। इसके प्रभाव से कई राज्यों में भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश, तेज हवाएं, आंधी और बिजली गिरने की घटनाएं हो सकती हैं। तमिलनाडु और केरल के कुछ इलाकों के लिए भारी बारिश का रेड अलर्ट भी बताया गया है। अगर आप आंध्र प्रदेश, ओडिशा, तमिलनाडु, केरल, बिहार या झारखंड में रहते हैं, तो मौसम विभाग की ताजा चेतावनियों पर नजर रखना जरूरी है। आइए जानते हैं कि किन राज्यों में बारिश का खतरा है और आने वाले दिनों में मौसम कैसा रह सकता है।
बंगाल की खाड़ी में बन सकता है चक्रवाती तूफान
मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, बंगाल की खाड़ी के ऊपर बना कम दबाव का क्षेत्र अगले कुछ दिनों में मजबूत हो सकता है। इसके 26 अक्टूबर तक चक्रवाती तूफान में बदलने की आशंका जताई गई है। इसके बाद यह सिस्टम 28 अक्टूबर के आसपास उत्तरी आंध्र प्रदेश और दक्षिणी ओडिशा के तटीय क्षेत्रों की ओर बढ़ सकता है। इसकी दिशा और तीव्रता के आधार पर बारिश और हवा के प्रभाव में बदलाव हो सकता है। आंध्र प्रदेश, ओडिशा, पश्चिम बंगाल, झारखंड, बिहार और छत्तीसगढ़ में बारिश की तीव्रता और समय अलग-अलग हो सकते हैं। इसलिए स्थानीय मौसम पूर्वानुमान को प्राथमिकता देना जरूरी है।
तमिलनाडु में भारी बारिश का अलर्ट, कई जिलों में सतर्कता
तमिलनाडु में अगले कुछ दिनों के दौरान कई इलाकों में भारी बारिश होने की संभावना जताई गई है। उपलब्ध मौसम अपडेट के अनुसार, विल्लुपुरम, कुड्डालोर, मयिलादुथुराई, नागपट्टिनम, तिरुवरुर, तंजावुर, कल्लाकुरिची, तिरुवन्नमलाई और कोयंबटूर सहित कई जिलों में बारिश का खतरा बताया गया है। इसके अलावा तिरुवल्लुर, चेन्नई, चेंगलपट्टू, कांचीपुरम, पुदुकोट्टई, वेल्लोर, रानीपेट, तिरुपत्तूर और अरियालुर में भी बारिश हो सकती है। थेनी, डिंडीगुल और मदुरै में भी सतर्क रहने की जरूरत है। पुडुचेरी और कराईकल में भी भारी से बहुत भारी बारिश की आशंका है। हालांकि, रेड अलर्ट किन जिलों में और किस समय लागू है, इसकी पुष्टि मौसम विभाग के ताजा जिला-वार बुलेटिन से करनी चाहिए।
केरल के इन जिलों में बहुत भारी बारिश की आशंका
केरल में भी बारिश का असर तेज हो सकता है। उपलब्ध अपडेट के अनुसार, 25 अक्टूबर को मलप्पुरम, कोझिकोड और वायनाड के लिए रेड अलर्ट बताया गया है। वहीं, 26 अक्टूबर को इडुक्की और पलक्कड़ में अत्यधिक भारी बारिश की चेतावनी दी गई है। इसके अलावा तिरुवनंतपुरम, कोल्लम, पथानामथिट्टा, अलाप्पुझा, कोट्टायम और एर्नाकुलम जैसे जिलों में भी बारिश को लेकर सतर्कता जरूरी है। भारी बारिश से निचले इलाकों में जलभराव, सड़क यातायात प्रभावित होने और पहाड़ी क्षेत्रों में भूस्खलन का खतरा बढ़ सकता है। स्थानीय प्रशासन के निर्देशों का पालन करना महत्वपूर्ण है।
आंध्र प्रदेश और ओडिशा में 27-28 अक्टूबर को बढ़ सकती है बारिश
चक्रवाती सिस्टम का संभावित असर आंध्र प्रदेश और ओडिशा के तटीय इलाकों में ज्यादा देखने को मिल सकता है। पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, आंध्र प्रदेश में 27 और 28 अक्टूबर को भारी बारिश हो सकती है। ओडिशा में 28 अक्टूबर के आसपास वर्षा की संभावना जताई गई है। तटीय इलाकों में रहने वाले लोगों को मौसम विभाग की चेतावनियों पर नजर रखनी चाहिए। मछुआरों और समुद्र में जाने की योजना बना रहे लोगों को स्थानीय प्रशासन तथा संबंधित विभागों के निर्देशों का पालन करना चाहिए।
बिहार और झारखंड में आंधी-तूफान की चेतावनी
बंगाल की खाड़ी में बनने वाले सिस्टम का प्रभाव पूर्वी भारत के राज्यों तक पहुंच सकता है। मौसम पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, 28 से 30 अक्टूबर के बीच पश्चिम बंगाल, बिहार और झारखंड के कुछ हिस्सों में भारी बारिश होने की संभावना है। 27 अक्टूबर को बिहार और झारखंड में 30 से 40 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से तेज हवाएं चल सकती हैं। कुछ स्थानों पर हवा की गति 50 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे तक पहुंचने की आशंका भी जताई गई है। उत्तर प्रदेश में 29 और 30 अक्टूबर को कुछ इलाकों में आंधी-तूफान के साथ बारिश हो सकती है। हालांकि, बारिश का सटीक स्थान और समय ताजा पूर्वानुमान के साथ बदल सकता है।
केरल, तमिलनाडु और अन्य राज्यों में भी बारिश
चक्रवाती सिस्टम के अलावा दक्षिण भारत के कुछ हिस्सों में भी बारिश की गतिविधियां जारी रह सकती हैं। उपलब्ध मौसम जानकारी के मुताबिक, केरल, तमिलनाडु, पुडुचेरी और कराईकल में कुछ स्थानों पर बहुत भारी बारिश का खतरा है। अंडमान और निकोबार द्वीप समूह, लक्षद्वीप तथा दक्षिण आंतरिक कर्नाटक में भी भारी वर्षा की संभावना जताई गई है। ऐसे में यात्रियों को सड़क, रेल और हवाई यात्रा से पहले मौसम तथा परिवहन संबंधी ताजा जानकारी देखनी चाहिए।
भारी बारिश और तेज हवाओं के दौरान क्या सावधानी रखें?
मौसम विभाग की चेतावनी के दौरान कुछ आसान सावधानियां जोखिम कम करने में मदद कर सकती हैं।
- मौसम अपडेट देखें: IMD और स्थानीय प्रशासन की ताजा चेतावनियों पर नजर रखें।
- जलभराव वाले रास्तों से बचें: पानी से भरी सड़कों या तेज बहाव वाले नालों को पार करने की कोशिश न करें।
- बिजली चमकने पर सुरक्षित रहें: खुले मैदान, पेड़ों और बिजली के खंभों से दूर रहें।
- ढीली वस्तुएं सुरक्षित करें: तेज हवाओं से उड़ सकने वाली चीजों को घर के अंदर रखें।
- तटीय इलाकों में सतर्क रहें: समुद्र में जाने से संबंधित आधिकारिक निर्देशों का पालन करें।
- यात्रा की योजना जांचें: खराब मौसम के दौरान यात्रा से पहले सड़क और परिवहन की स्थिति पता करें।

articles.title: बस्तर संभाग में 27 से 29 अक्टूबर तक हाेगी भारी बारिश, रेड अलर्ट जारी - Vocal TV

बस्तर संभाग में 27 से 29 अक्टूबर तक हाेगी भारी बारिश, रेड अलर्ट जारी
जगदलपुर, 25 अक्टूबर (हि.स.)। बंगाल की खाड़ी में बन रहे एक नया मौसम सिस्टम के कारण बस्तर में 27 से 29 अक्टूबर को मूसलाधार बारिश हो सकती है। ने बस्तर संभाग के लिए रेड अलर्ट जारी किया है।
बस्तर में कुछ जगहों पर 204 मिमी. से अधिक बारिश हो सकती है, भारी बारिश जनजीवन को प्रभावित कर सकती है। बस्तर, दंतेवाड़ा और सुकमा में भारी बारिश होगी, कांकेर और बीजापुर में भी अलर्ट जारी है। कोंडागांव और नारायणपुर में सतर्कता बरतने की सलाह मौसम विभाग ने दी है।
बंगाल की खाड़ी में कम दबाव का क्षेत्र बन चुका है, यह जल्द ही अवदाब में बदल जाएगा। इसके बाद यह गहरे अवदाब का रूप लेगा। गहरे अवदाब से 26 अक्टूबर तक यह चक्रवाती तूफान बन सकता है। इस तूफान का असर पूरे छत्तीसगढ़ पर पड़ेगा, जिसका सबसे अधिक असर बस्तर संभाग में पड़ेगा। मौसम विभाग ने रविवार काे पत्र भेजकर बस्तर संभाग के लिए रेड अलर्ट जारी किया है, आपदा प्रबंधन टीम को अलर्ट पर रखा गया है। आने वाले कुछ दिनों तक ठंड नहीं बढ़ेगी, आसमान में घने बादल छाए रहेंगे। बादलों के कारण न्यूनतम तापमान बढ़ेगा।
---------------
हिन्दुस्थान समाचार / राकेश पांडे

Women were losing 23% of their income to extreme heat. This engineer fought back
Bijal Brahmbhatt had no fixed career plan after graduating as a civil engineer in 1992. Today, she leads Mahila Housing Trust, an Earthshot Prize 2026 finalist helping low-income women tackle extreme heat through cool roofs, climate insurance and community-led action. Her journey transformed how she understands engineering and urban development.

Bijal Brahmbhatt leads Mahila Housing Trust, an Earthshot Prize 2026 finalist helping low-income women tackle extreme heat through cool roofs, climate insurance and community-led action.
When Bijal Brahmbhatt graduated as a civil engineer in 1992, she thought engineering happened on drawing boards and construction sites. More than three decades later, she knows some of the most important urban planning decisions can begin in a women's meeting in a slum, where residents decide which problem to take to the authorities first.
That change in perspective has shaped her life's work. As director of Ahmedabad-based Mahila Housing Trust (MHT), Brahmbhatt is helping low-income women tackle extreme heat through reflective roofs, community-led Heat Action Plans and climate insurance.
The organisation has been named one of India's two finalists for the 2026 Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William.
The recognition comes as the environmental award arrives in India for the first time. The five winners will be announced in Mumbai on November 17.
But Brahmbhatt's story is not simply about an engineer who found her calling in climate action. It is about a professional who learnt that technical expertise means little if it ignores the people whose lives a solution is supposed to improve.
THE ENGINEER WHO HAD TO LEARN FROM MASONS
"Like most young people graduating at that time, I did not really know what I wanted my career, or my life, to look like. I tried different things,” she says, in a conversation with India Today Digital.
After graduating in 1992, Brahmbhatt taught students preparing to become engineers before moving to construction sites. At a time when women engineers on-site were rare, employers hesitated to send her there, citing safety concerns. A smaller company eventually gave her the opportunity through a professor's reference.
"I was young, rebellious and constantly questioning things, particularly around what could make the world a more just place for women," she recalls.
Her two years with a private construction firm brought an education of their own. Conversations sometimes stopped when she entered a site. Some workers looked at her with curiosity, others with amusement.
She also discovered how much her degree had left out.
"I may have been the supervisor, but there were things I had to learn from the mason. If you are doing carpentry, the carpenter is your teacher. Your degree cannot teach you everything. That brought a lot of humility."
The experience left her questioning not just who got taken seriously in a male-dominated profession, but what engineering was supposed to achieve in the first place.
"In college, we learnt to calculate loads and design structures, but nobody really asked us who would live in those buildings or what their lives would be like."
That question would follow her into a very different kind of workplace.
A HOUSE IS MORE THAN WALLS AND A ROOF
In 1998, Brahmbhatt's father, an academic involved in the voluntary sector, introduced her to Renana Jhabvala of the Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA). Jhabvala proposed that she join Mahila Housing Trust, an independent organisation working on the housing and habitat needs of low-income women.
"I still remember being surprised by how quickly she trusted me. By the end of our first conversation, she had asked me to join MHT," she says.
The organisation was then working in just three slum communities in Ahmedabad, with two other staff members besides Brahmbhatt.
"There was no blueprint. The idea was to listen to what women needed and work from there."
The women she met began changing how she understood a house. For an engineer, it might be a structure with a foundation, walls and a roof. For a woman earning a living from home, it could also be a workshop, a storehouse and a productive asset.

"She may stitch garments, roll agarbattis or pack goods there. So, a leaking roof or poor ventilation is not just a housing problem; it can directly affect her income," she explains.
Brahmbhatt also found an organisation where marriage and motherhood did not have to compete with professional ambition. She had married and started a family around the time she joined MHT.
"It was a women's organisation, but it was never anti-men. It was feminist without having to constantly say that it was feminist."
That experience shaped her understanding of what an empowered woman could look like. At MHT, she learnt to listen before designing and to recognise that people who experience a problem often understand its complexities better than an outsider.

WHEN WOMEN MADE THE COST OF HEAT VISIBLE
Around 2015, the women MHT worked with began speaking increasingly about extreme heat. Homes with metal-sheet or concrete roofs and little ventilation were becoming unbearable during summer.
The effects reached far beyond discomfort. Women were losing working hours, spending more on electricity and cold drinking water, and taking on additional care responsibilities for children and older family members.
"What struck me was that many women simply accepted heat as part of summer. Some even described it as an act of God. So, we felt we needed to make this invisible problem visible."
MHT trained women to use temperature loggers in their homes and began documenting the economic cost of rising temperatures. Women reported losing 23 per cent of their income during the hot season, while their expenses increased, Brahmbhatt says.
"Once you put those numbers alongside a woman trying to work at her sewing machine under a hot roof, heat is no longer just an environmental issue. It becomes an issue of health, livelihoods and economic security."
That evidence changed how MHT approached the problem. Reflective cool roofs could reduce indoor temperatures by up to 5°C, but cooling a house would not compensate a woman for wages lost when the heat made working impossible.
"A heat alert might advise people to stay indoors, but for many women, indoors can be the hottest place because they live under metal sheet or concrete roofs. And staying home does not mean they can stop working. If they stop working, they lose income," she says.
MHT subsequently developed parametric heat insurance with its partners. When an agreed temperature threshold is crossed, a fixed payment is triggered without requiring women to file a traditional claim or prove their individual losses.
Brahmbhatt says around 2,000 women policyholders received payouts in 2024 after the threshold was breached. She puts the current reach of the insurance at 49,000 women in Delhi and Gujarat.
"What women have taught us is that climate protection has to address both the home and the household budget."
THE WOMEN WHO BECAME THEIR OWN URBAN PLANNERS
One of Brahmbhatt's most telling examples of community leadership comes from Odhav ward in Ahmedabad.
A group of women trained by MHT identified the need for a bus stop in their area. Led by Minaben, they surveyed around 1,000 households, mapped GPS data to build their case and approached middle-class households outside the settlement, securing consent from around 400 of them.
They then kept following up with the authorities until the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation accepted their application and built the bus stop.
"None of these women had a degree in urban planning, but what they did was exactly what a good planner would do: gather evidence, build support and navigate the system."
For Brahmbhatt, this is what community-led development can achieve when women have access to information and the tools to make their case. The women were not simply receiving a service. They were identifying a need, gathering evidence and negotiating with the institution responsible for addressing it.
"Leadership does not necessarily come from education, designation or social background. It comes from within," she says.
The challenge is getting governments to treat such solutions as part of urban planning rather than welfare work. MHT's work in Jodhpur helped inform a Heat Action Plan that included cool roofs, cooling shelters, parks and green spaces, with vulnerable wards prioritised.
Brahmbhatt says its cooling shelter model influenced Rajasthan's decision to build 41 shelters, while Maharashtra now supports heat insurance for women living below the poverty line.
Yet getting a successful pilot adopted is only the beginning. Government officers change, priorities shift and programmes can lose momentum.
"A pilot is relatively easy. Getting a city to adopt it, fund it and sustain it is the real work."
WHAT ENGINEERING MEANS TO HER NOW
MHT aims to protect three million households with cool roofs by 2030 and reach 300,000 women with climate insurance, according to Brahmbhatt. The Earthshot recognition could help the organisation build partnerships and expand its model.
But she sees the achievement as belonging to the women who helped develop it.
In 1992, she could not have imagined working with insurers, researchers and city governments on temperature thresholds, weather data and climate resilience. Nor could she have predicted how much she would learn from women whose technical qualifications might not match her own.
Today, those women are collecting heat data to inform city-level action plans and even helping ground-truth AI models.
"In an age where we are increasingly talking about artificial intelligence, we should not lose the human intelligence and lived experience that these women bring."
It is perhaps the clearest expression of how far her understanding of engineering has travelled. The profession still needs technical knowledge, data and sound design. But Brahmbhatt believes those things work best when the people living with the problem help shape the answer.
Her advice to young women engineers is equally direct.
"You will sometimes be underestimated. Let that make you better at your work, never smaller."

As temperatures rise across parts of Nigeria, health authorities are warning residents to take precautions against the effects of extreme heat.
The warning comes as the country moves from the rainy season into the hotter, drier months, when prolonged exposure to high temperatures can increase the risk of dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke.
A recent report by the Climate Impact Lab estimated that Nigeria could record 31,400 additional heat-related deaths between September 2026 and February 2027.
The report, titled “451,000 at Risk: Where Action Can Save Lives During the Super El Niño,” estimated 451,000 additional heat-related deaths globally during the period.
The Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet), in a 23 October advisory, also warned of hotter days and increased heat discomfort as the country enters the dry season.
The agency said changing weather conditions, including reduced rainfall and cloud cover, could contribute to rising temperatures. It warned that excessive heat could cause dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke.
People most at risk
Extreme heat can affect anyone, but some people are more vulnerable to its effects.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) identifies older people, young children, people with chronic illnesses and outdoor workers among those who face greater health risks during periods of extreme heat.
People living with heart, lung or kidney conditions, diabetes and other chronic illnesses may also experience worsening symptoms when temperatures become very high.
Outdoor workers, including farmers, construction workers, traders and others who spend long periods under the sun, can also be exposed to heat for several hours without adequate opportunities to cool down.
WHO said extreme heat places additional stress on the body as it tries to maintain a normal temperature. Prolonged exposure can increase the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke and may also worsen existing health conditions.
What should you do?
NiMet advised Nigerians to drink water regularly and wear lightweight, breathable clothing.
It said people should also limit prolonged exposure to direct sunlight, particularly during the hottest periods of the day, and strenuous physical activities should be moved to cooler hours.
NiMet further urged schools and workplaces to ensure adequate ventilation, provide drinking water and shaded rest areas, and allow regular breaks during hot weather.
WHO similarly advises people to avoid strenuous activity during the hottest part of the day, stay in shaded or cool places and keep their homes as cool as possible.
People should also check on relatives, neighbours and friends who may be more vulnerable, particularly older people and those living alone.
WHO urged parents to take extra care with young children. Children should not be left alone in parked vehicles, as temperatures inside vehicles can rise rapidly even when the weather outside does not appear extreme.
Warning signs
Symptoms of heat exhaustion may include heavy sweating, weakness, headache, dizziness and nausea. Moving the person to a cooler place, giving fluids where they are able to drink and helping them cool down can help prevent the condition from becoming more serious.
Heatstroke is different and requires urgent medical attention. According to WHO, heatstroke is a potentially fatal medical emergency. Someone with hot, dry skin, delirium, convulsions or loss of consciousness during extreme heat should receive immediate medical attention.
The Climate Impact Lab said the projections provide an opportunity for governments and humanitarian organisations to identify vulnerable populations and direct resources towards interventions that can save lives.
NiMet has also urged Nigerians to follow official weather forecasts and advisories as conditions change.

25 October, 2026Garaad Jaamac Garaad Cali ayaa sheegay in taageerada dadka Soomaaliyeed ee ku nool Mooyaale ay waajib ku tahay dhammaan ummadda Soomaaliyeed, isaga oo carrabka ku adkeeyay muhiimadda ay leedahay garab istaagga dadka Soomaaliyeed meel kasta oo ay joogaan.
Garaad Jaamac ayaa adkeeyey midnimada, walaaltinimada iyo iskaashiga bulshada Soomaaliyeed, gaar ahaan marka ay jiraan duruufo u baahan in dadka la garab istaago, isagoo muujiyey in xiriirka ka dhexeeya dadka Soomaaliyeed uusan ku koobnayn xuduudaha deegaannada ay ku nool yihiin, balse ay muhiim tahay in la muujiyo isku duubni iyo taageero loo fidiyo dadka Soomaaliyeed ee u baahan garab istaag.
“Taageerada dadka Soomaaliyeed ee Mooyaale waa ku waajib dhamaan umada Soomaaliyeed; Geed iyo Guri midna inama dheera”, Ayuu yiri Garaad Jaamac Garaad Cali.
Degmada Mooyaale ee dowlad deegaanka Soomaalida Itoobiya ayaa muddooyinkii dambe waxaa ka socdey dadka deegaanka iyo ciidamada qoomiyadda Oromada Itoobiya oo diiddan in calanka Soomaalida laga taago degmadaasi iyo tuulooyinka hoos yimaada.
